This report delivers a comprehensive legal, financial, and technical audit of the research and development (R&D) tax incentive architecture of Canada as of November 2026.

The Canadian R&D tax landscape has undergone its most substantial statutory expansion in over a decade following the enactment of Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, and applies retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Key structural reforms include doubling the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35 per cent refundable Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3.0 million to $6.0 million—yielding a maximum annual federal cash refund of $2.1 million and superseding the $4.5 million interim proposal in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement; widening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historic $10 million–$50 million corridor to $15 million–$75 million; extending the enhanced 35 per cent refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15 million–$75 million) that Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) may also elect to use; and restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and lease costs for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an elective pre-claim approval process that provides upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and reduces post-filing expenditure review processing times from 180 days to 90 days. At the provincial level, Quebec enacted Bill 6 (S.Q. 2025, c. 35), replacing its four legacy R&D tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, with the unified, refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (also designated the tax credit for R&D, innovation and pre-commercialization), which provides a 30 per cent rate on the first $1.0 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20 per cent thereafter.
1. Executive Summary and National R&D Fiscal Architecture

Canada operates one of the most heavily tax-weighted innovation support systems among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) nations, delivering approximately 84 per cent of its federal R&D business support through indirect tax incentives rather than direct discretionary grants. The cornerstone of this regime is the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, which is jointly architected by the Department of Finance Canada—which formulates legislative policy under the Income Tax Act (ITA) and Income Tax Regulations (ITR)—and administered operationally by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA).

In fiscal year 2024–2025, the federal SR&ED program delivered $4.5 billion in investment tax credits to more than 19,000 claimants across over 22,000 processed claims. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, total SR&ED investment tax credits claimed rose to $4.9 billion, with $4.6 billion allowed by the CRA—representing a cumulative climb of roughly 50 per cent in credit value since fiscal year 2022. Contrary to persistent industry perceptions that SR&ED claims face high rejection rates during audit, CRA administration figures reported in industry analyses for the most recent reporting year indicate that roughly 96 per cent of SR&ED claims result in allowed tax credits: 90 per cent of claims are accepted as filed, 6 per cent are accepted following audit modifications, and only 4 per cent (approximately 1 in 25 claims) are denied in full.

The federal SR&ED program provides two distinct, complementary statutory tax incentives under the Income Tax Act. First, under subsection 37(1), taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada may pool allowable current SR&ED expenditures—and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, allowable capital SR&ED expenditures—in a dedicated pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. This pool may be deducted in full or in part to reduce net business income for tax purposes in the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in any subsequent taxation year. Second, under section 127 and section 127.1, claimants earn an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a percentage (35 per cent enhanced rate or 15 per cent basic rate) of their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year. Depending on the taxpayer's legal classification, prior-year taxable capital or three-year average gross revenue, and expenditure nature (current versus capital), unused ITCs may be refunded directly in cash, applied to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable, carried back three taxation years, or carried forward up to 20 taxation years.

body.text: 2. Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Technical Eligibility Framework
2.1 Subsection 248(1) Statutory Definition

Unlike jurisdictions that maintain separate science-ministry definitions for R&D grants versus tax deductions, Canada anchors all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives—with the exception of Quebec's supplemental pre-commercialization stream under the new CRIC—in a single statutory definition located in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Under subsection 248(1), "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statutory definition is structured into three operational tiers: three core research and development categories (paragraphs (a), (b), and (c)), one derivative support work category (paragraph (d)), and seven explicit statutory exclusions (paragraphs (e) through (k)).
Core Qualifying Research Categories (Paragraphs 248(1)(a)–(c))

Under subsection 248(1), the three core categories of eligible work are basic research, applied research, and experimental development. Basic research (paragraph 248(1)(a)) comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Applied research (paragraph 248(1)(b)) comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Experimental development (paragraph 248(1)(c)) comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Most commercial business SR&ED claims in Canada fall under paragraph (c) as experimental development, including incremental improvements to existing shop-floor manufacturing processes or software architectures.
Derivative Support Work Category (Paragraph 248(1)(d))

Under paragraph 248(1)(d), SR&ED includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive statutory categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research. Work falling within these eight categories does not constitute SR&ED on a standalone basis. To qualify under paragraph 248(1)(d), the support work must satisfy a dual nexus requirement: it must be (i) commensurate with the needs, and (ii) directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development (described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c)) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.
Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs 248(1)(e)–(k))
Subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes from the definition of SR&ED any work with respect to seven enumerated non-qualifying activities:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph (j): Style changes; and
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection.

body.text: As clarified by the CRA's eligibility guidelines, the presence of an excluded activity within a broader commercial endeavour—for example, mineral prospecting under paragraph (h) or commercial production runs under paragraph (i)—does not taint or disqualify concurrent experimental development performed on the same site, provided the claimant isolates the eligible experimental development and support work from the excluded commercial activities. Furthermore, distinguishing between eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as "testing" or "data collection") and excluded work under paragraphs (f) and (k) ("routine testing" or "routine data collection") turns entirely on the purpose of the activity: if data collection or testing is carried out specifically for the purpose of performing basic research, applied research, or experimental development, it qualifies as paragraph (d) support work.
2.2 CRA's "Why" and "How" Eligibility Framework (August 2021 Guidelines)

On August 13, 2021, the CRA archived its former Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (which was structured around five sequential evaluation questions) and replaced it with the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. As the CRA and the Federal Court of Appeal (in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72) have both emphasized, the 2021 Guidelines did not alter the legal definition under subsection 248(1) or the common-law criteria established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839). Instead, the CRA consolidated the five Northwest Hydraulic questions into two overarching, mandatory requirements—the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement.
1. The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty)

The "Why" requirement evaluates the underlying objective of the work: it must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. The CRA distinguishes between generating conceptual knowledge—such as theories or predictive models explaining how or why a phenomenon, material, or system behaves—and merely gathering factual knowledge, such as routine measurements or parameter readings. New scientific or technological knowledge is needed only when it is uncertain whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, due to an insufficiency in the available scientific or technological knowledge base, which encompasses both publicly accessible sources and the combined knowledge and experience within the claimant's business.

In experimental development projects, the CRA's guidelines identify eight practical indicators that available technological knowledge is insufficient: existing design methods are not applicable; requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; too many variables or unknowns exist; parameters or conditions fall outside normal operating ranges; the nature of the problem is evolving; required data is not readily available; interlocking constraints exist; or technological uncertainty arises when attempting to achieve technical objectives constrained by reasonable cost targets. (However, as established by the Tax Court of Canada in 6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 17, framing a project's uncertainty solely as a cost-efficiency target without an underlying technological obstacle does not qualify as SR&ED.) Acquiring existing knowledge or know-how through staff training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not satisfy the "Why" requirement. Similarly, circumventing a technological uncertainty using an available workaround rather than addressing the underlying knowledge gap fails the "Why" test. Conversely, success or failure in meeting the ultimate commercial goal is irrelevant: if a systematic investigation proves that a hypothesized approach will not work, rejecting that hypothesis still counts as a technological advancement because it eliminates a possible solution and generates new technological knowledge.
2. The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search)

The "How" requirement governs the methodology used to resolve the scientific or technological uncertainty. Simply working systematically, following a structured project plan, or applying established engineering design protocols is insufficient. Under the CRA Guidelines, a qualifying systematic investigation or search requires four mandatory methodological steps:

items: Formulating a Hypothesis (Idea): Generating an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward achieving the objective or resolving the problem, expressed as a proposed method, approach, or possible solution.
Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change as a result of testing.

Developing Logical Conclusions: Drawing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis, including analysing why an option failed before testing subsequent modifications.
Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: Maintaining dated records and evidence that are generated as the work progresses, rather than reconstructing narratives after the fact.

body.text: 3. Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures
3.1 Mechanics of the Subsection 37(1) Expenditure Pool

Under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct expenditures of a current nature (under paragraph 37(1)(a)) and—following the enactment of Bill C-15 for property acquired after December 15, 2024—expenditures of a capital nature (under restored paragraph 37(1)(b)) incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada that relate to a business of the taxpayer. Rather than deducting these expenses under ordinary business income rules, qualifying SR&ED expenditures are accumulated in a running Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures calculated in Section C of Part 3 of Form T661.

Under subsection 37(1.1), when a corporate claimant performs SR&ED related to a business actively engaged in by a related corporation (such as a wholly owned subsidiary performing SR&ED related to its parent company's business), the SR&ED is considered related to a business of the claimant provided the related corporation is actively engaged in that business at the time the expenditure is incurred or paid. Additionally, under subsection 37(1.3), SR&ED carried on in Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone is included within the scope of SR&ED carried on in Canada. While current expenditures incurred for SR&ED performed outside Canada (under subsection 37(2)) may be deducted when calculating net income or loss for general tax purposes, they cannot be included in the Section 37 pool on Form T661 or earn ITCs, except for permissible outside-Canada employee salaries under subsection 37(1.5). Under subsection 37(4) and paragraph 2902(c) of the Income Tax Regulations, no deduction is allowed for an expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED. Furthermore, under subsection 37(5), if an expenditure in respect of SR&ED could otherwise be deductible both as an SR&ED expenditure and as a charitable donation under section 110.1 or 118.1, it must be deducted under section 37 as an SR&ED expenditure and not as a charitable gift.
Statutory Additions to the Pool (Subsection 37(1))
The pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is increased each taxation year by six statutory categories:

items: Prior-Year Undeducted Pool Balance: The positive balance of deductible SR&ED expenditures carried forward from the preceding taxation year (Line 450 of Form T661).

Current SR&ED Expenditures in Canada (Paragraph 37(1)(a)): Allowable current expenditures incurred in the taxation year, comprising the eligible portion of salaries or wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED, the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED, lease costs of equipment used for SR&ED incurred after December 15, 2024 (or prior to 2014), contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant, eligible third-party payments to corporations and approved entities, and—only when the Traditional Method is used—allowable SR&ED overhead and other expenditures. (When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is a notional figure used solely to earn ITCs and is never added to the Section 37 deductible pool).

Capital SR&ED Expenditures in Canada (Paragraph 37(1)(b)): Allowable expenditures of a capital nature for new or used depreciable property (excluding buildings and leasehold interests in buildings) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (or prior to 2014), that meet the "all or substantially all" (≥90%) operating-time or value-consumed intention test (Line 390 of Form T661). Under subsection 37(6), an SR&ED capital expenditure deduction claimed from the pool is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA).

Repayments of Assistance (Paragraph 37(1)(c)): Repayments of government assistance or non-government assistance made in the year that had previously reduced the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (Line 445 of Form T661).
Prior-Year Negative Pool Income Inclusions (Paragraph 37(1)(c.1)): Amounts included in the claimant's income in a previous taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v) due to a negative pool balance.

Amalgamation/Wind-Up Transfers and Prior-Year ITC Recapture (Paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and 37(1)(c.3)): Pool balances transferred on an amalgamation or wind-up (Line 452 of Form T661), as well as the amount of SR&ED ITC recaptured in the prior taxation year or partnership ITC recapture excess amounts (Line 453 of Form T661).

body.text: Statutory Reductions to the Pool (Subsection 37(1))
Before computing the optional deduction for the year, the Section 37 pool is decreased by five statutory categories:

items: Government and Non-Government Assistance (Paragraph 37(1)(d)): All provincial or territorial government assistance (such as the Ontario OITC/ORDTC or Quebec CRIC), other government assistance (such as NRC IRAP grants), and non-government assistance (inducements, subsidies, forgivable loans) that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for expenditures included in the pool (Lines 429, 431, and 432 of Form T661).
Super-Allowance Benefit Amount (Paragraph 37(1)(d.1)): Any provincial "super-allowance benefit amount" for the year or preceding taxation years.

Prior-Year Federal SR&ED ITCs Applied or Refunded (Paragraph 37(1)(e)): The total federal SR&ED ITCs applied against Part I tax (including carrybacks) and/or refunded in cash in a preceding taxation year (Line 435 of Form T661). Because federal ITCs reduce the Section 37 pool in the taxation year following the year they are claimed or refunded, they reduce the subsequent year's available SR&ED deduction rather than grinding the current year's ITC base.

Prior-Year Deductions and Insolvency Reductions (Paragraphs 37(1)(f) and 37(1)(f.1)): Amounts deducted from the pool under subsection 37(1) in preceding taxation years, and amounts deducted with respect to insolvency under section 61.3 in preceding years.

Sale of SR&ED Capital Assets and Loss Restriction Reductions (Line 440 & Paragraph 37(1)(h)): Adjustments for the sale of SR&ED capital assets and pool reductions required under subsection 37(6.1) upon a loss restriction event.

body.text: If the statutory reductions to the pool in a taxation year exceed the opening pool balance and current-year additions, the resulting negative pool balance must be included in the taxpayer's income for the year under paragraph 12(1)(v), and that income inclusion is then added back to restore the pool to nil in the following year under paragraph 37(1)(c.1).
3.2 Indefinite Carryforward, Partnerships, and Loss Restriction Events

A positive balance in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (Line 470 of Form T661) does not expire. Because claiming a deduction from the pool in any given year is optional (Line 460), a corporate claimant can carry forward its undeducted pool balance indefinitely as a running total and deduct all or any portion of it against business income in any subsequent taxation year. Moreover, once SR&ED expenditures have been properly identified on Form T661 by the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline for the year incurred, the subsequent deduction of those pooled amounts in a later taxation year is not subject to the SR&ED reporting deadline.

Two strict statutory restrictions govern partnerships and corporate acquisitions of control. First, under paragraph 96(1)(e.1) and the CRA's SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy, a partnership cannot carry forward a pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent fiscal period. Consequently, the entire balance of a partnership's Section 37 pool at the end of its fiscal period must be fully deducted when calculating the partnership's net income or loss for that year. Furthermore, under the partnership loss restriction rules for limited partners, any portion of a partnership loss that is disallowed to a limited partner because it includes a deduction for SR&ED expenditures is not allowed to other partners, does not become a limited partnership loss or a non-capital loss, and does not reduce the adjusted cost base of the limited partner's partnership interest.

Second, under subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h), when a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (or a trust has a new majority-interest beneficiary), a loss restriction event occurs: there is a deemed taxation year-end immediately before the acquisition of control, and the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is reduced to nil. The undeducted pool balance from before the loss restriction event may be reinstated and carried forward for deduction in a subsequent taxation year only if (1) the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related is continued for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and (2) the deduction is limited to the extent of the taxpayer's income for the taxation year (before making any Section 37 pool deduction) from that same business or a similar business.
4. Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Regime and the 2024–2026 Reforms
4.1 Legislative Timeline: From the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026)

When auditing Canadian R&D tax documentation prepared between late 2024 and 2026, tax practitioners must distinguish between the interim legislative proposals of December 2024 and the final statutory parameters enacted into law in March 2026:

items: 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) & Draft Legislation (August 15, 2025): The Department of Finance initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the 35 per cent enhanced refundable ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million (which would have provided up to $1.575 million in annual refundable ITCs), increasing the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from 10M–50M to 15M–75M, extending the 35 per cent enhanced credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) via a 15M–75M three-year average gross revenue phase-out, and restoring capital expenditure eligibility for property acquired after December 15, 2024. Draft legislative proposals were released by the Department of Finance on August 15, 2025, for public consultation through September 12, 2025.

Federal Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025) & Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026): On November 4, 2025, the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, François-Philippe Champagne, presented Budget 2025, which confirmed all structural SR&ED measures from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and further increased the annual enhanced ITC expenditure limit from $4.5 million to $6.0 million. Enacted via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the $6.0 million expenditure limit (allowing up to $2.1 million annually in refundable federal ITCs) and all associated program expansions are now law and apply retroactively to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024).

body.text: 4.2 Basic (15%) and Enhanced (35%) ITC Rates and Eligible Entities

Under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), an SR&ED ITC is earned at either the basic rate of 15 per cent or the enhanced rate of 35 per cent on a claimant's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year. (No ITC may be earned on an SR&ED expenditure incurred in the course of earning income that is exempt from Part I tax under subsection 149(1), which excludes Crown corporations other than Prescribed Federal Crown Corporations under Regulation 7100.)
1. Enhanced Investment Tax Credit Rate (35%)

The enhanced ITC rate of 35 per cent (comprising the 15 per cent basic rate plus an additional 20 per cent enhancement) is earned on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the claimant's annual expenditure limit—a maximum threshold of $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 ($3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024). For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, two categories of corporations qualify to earn the 35 per cent enhanced rate:

items: Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs): Qualifying CCPCs earn the 35 per cent rate up to their expenditure limit (shared among associated CCPCs via Schedule T2SCH49).

Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs): Defined in subsection 127(9) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an ECPC is a corporation that, throughout the taxation year, satisfies three statutory criteria: (1) it is resident in Canada; (2) it has a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or has elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and (3) it is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. In addition, Canadian-resident subsidiary corporations where all or substantially all (90 per cent or more) of the shares are owned by one or more ECPCs are also eligible for the enhanced refundable ITC, sharing the expenditure limit across the corporate group.

body.text: 2. Basic Investment Tax Credit Rate (15%)

The basic SR&ED ITC rate of 15 per cent applies to corporations other than qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs (such as foreign-controlled corporations and large public corporations), to CCPCs and ECPCs on qualified SR&ED expenditures in excess of their annual expenditure limit, and to sole proprietorships (individuals), partners of a partnership (allocated under subsection 127(8), excluding "specified members" who are passive/limited partners precluded from receiving partnership SR&ED ITCs), and beneficiaries of trusts.
4.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital vs. Elective Gross Revenue

Under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.5) of the Income Tax Act, the maximum $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, is prorated for short taxation years based on the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365, and is subject to a gradual reduction (phase-out) based on either prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada or three-year average annual gross revenue. (Special allocation rules under subsection 127(10.5) also apply when a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated with another CCPC.)
Method A: Prior-Year Taxable Capital Phase-Out (Default for CCPCs)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit of a CCPC (and all associated CCPCs) begins to decrease when the taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year reaches $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated (becomes nil) when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000. (For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3,000,000 expenditure limit began decreasing at $10,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital and became nil at $50,000,000.) Across the $60,000,000 phase-out range between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit decreases on a straight-line basis by $0.10 for every $1.00 of prior-year taxable capital exceeding $15,000,000 (whereas under the interim $4.5 million limit proposed in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, the reduction rate was $0.075 per $1.00 of taxable capital above $15,000,000).
Method B: Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out (Mandatory for ECPCs, Elective for CCPCs)

For an ECPC, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when its average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, reaching nil at $75,000,000. For standalone entities, gross revenue is taken from the annual financial statements prepared in accordance with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) and presented to shareholders. Where an ECPC is a member of a corporate group preparing consolidated financial statements, gross revenue must be calculated using the total average annual revenue reflected in the consolidated financial statements presented to shareholders at the highest level of consolidation for each member of the group over the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout that entire period. Crucially, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC may elect on its prescribed form to calculate its expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average annual gross revenue method instead of the taxable capital method, allowing each CCPC to select whichever structure yields the higher expenditure limit.
4.4 Refundability Mechanics and the Qualifying Income Limit (Section 127.1)

Under section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act (specifically subsections 127.1(2), 127.1(2.01), and 127.1(3)), a claimant that has no federal Part I tax otherwise payable may receive all or part of its unclaimed current-year SR&ED ITCs as a cash refund. Under subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC refunded in the taxation year is deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable, which reduces the ITCs available for carryback or carryforward and triggers a reduction to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e).

To determine whether a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) (which governs whether it receives a 40 per cent cash refund on basic 15 per cent ITCs earned above the expenditure limit), the corporation's prior-year taxable income (combined across all associated corporations) must not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit. Consequential on the Bill C-15 amendments to subsection 127(10.2), for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Qualifying Income Limit formula in subsection 127.1(2) is updated to align with the $15 million to $75 million taxable capital corridor:

items: Post-December 15, 2024 Qualifying Income Limit Formula: Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (on an associated basis) is $15,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.

(For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the formula was $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000], where reduction began above $10,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital and reached nil at $50,000,000).

body.text: Furthermore, consequential on the restoration of paragraph 37(1)(b) for capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024, subparagraph (f)(i) of the definition of "refundable investment tax credit" in subsection 127.1(2) was amended to add the exclusion "(other than expenditures of a capital nature)" to the 100 per cent refundability tier, thereby setting the cash refundability rate for SR&ED capital expenditures at 40 per cent even when the credit is earned at the enhanced 35 per cent rate.

body.text: 4.5 Carryback, Carryforward, and Investment Tax Credit Recapture (Subsections 127(27)–(36))

Unused current-year SR&ED ITCs that are not refunded in cash or applied to offset Part I tax in the current year may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (limited to the lesser of the undeducted current-year ITC and the Part I tax otherwise payable in that prior year net of prior ITCs) or carried forward for up to 20 taxation years. An acquisition of control restricts the carryforward and carryback of unused ITCs.

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, an SR&ED ITC is recaptured and added to Part I tax payable (calculated on Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) when four cumulative conditions are met: (1) the claimant acquired a particular property from a person or partnership in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years in paragraph 127(27)(a) to 20 years by subsection 127(36) for ITCs earned in 1998 and subsequent years); (2) the cost of the property was a qualified SR&ED expenditure; (3) a percentage of the property's cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC; and (4) in the taxation year, the claimant converts to commercial use or disposes of the particular property or another property incorporating it.

Property subject to ITC recapture includes materials transformed that are incorporated into a custom product, commercial asset, or experimental/commercial production run, all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) SR&ED capital equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), animals and growing things used in SR&ED projects, and physical property acquired under an arm's-length SR&ED contract. For recapture purposes, the cost of the property cannot exceed the amount paid to acquire it from another person and excludes internal labour or costs incurred by the claimant to modify or transform the property. Conversely, salaries and wages, overhead, materials consumed (rendered valueless), and SR&ED contracts generating intellectual property (IP) never trigger ITC recapture when the resulting IP is sold or converted to commercial use. In a partnership (subsections 127(28), 127(30), 127(31), and 127(35)), ITC recapture first reduces the partnership's current-year SR&ED ITC allocation to partners, and any excess recapture is added directly to the partners' Part I tax payable.
5. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
5.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) vs. (B))

Under subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy (updated March 30, 2022), a claimant must select either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method on a year-by-year basis on Form T661. If the claimant elects the Proxy Method (by checking Line 160 of Form T661 and completing Part 5), overhead and other indirect expenditures are not tracked or added to the Section 37 deductible pool (Line 360 is entered as "0", and actual overhead is deducted as an ordinary business expense). Instead, the claimant calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations equal to 55 per cent of its eligible SR&ED salary base (reduced from 65 per cent before 2013 to 60 per cent in 2013 and 55 per cent after 2013) and includes the PPA on Line 502 of Form T661 to earn SR&ED ITCs.

If the claimant selects the Traditional Method (by checking Line 162 of Form T661, or by default if no election is made on Line 160), the claimant does not compute a PPA (entering "0" on Line 502) and instead specifically identifies, tracks, and allocates actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 that are either all or substantially all (≥90%) attributable or directly attributable (both directly related and incremental under Regulations 2900(2) and 2900(3)) to the prosecution of SR&ED or the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED in Canada. Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that year and cannot be changed after the SR&ED reporting deadline.

body.text: 5.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, and YMPE Caps

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" is defined in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act as the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act. Allowable SR&ED salary or wages include regular salary, wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, inducements, non-competition payments, and (for non-specified employees only) bonuses and qualifying taxable benefits. Allowable salaries strictly exclude the employer's share of related benefits (such as employer CPP, EI, or pension contributions), extended vacation or extended sick leave, stock option benefits, retiring allowances, any GST/HST or PST component on taxable benefits for which the employer claims an input tax credit under subsection 248(16), and any salary or wages paid to a partner of a partnership (since a partner cannot be an employee of the partnership for income tax purposes, and such payments are treated as distributions of partnership income).

Only the portion of an employee's salary or wages reasonably attributable to hands-on time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada can be claimed on Lines 300 and 305 of Form T661 (though if a non-specified employee spends all or substantially all—90 per cent or more—of their time directly engaged in SR&ED, 100 per cent of their salary is deemed eligible under clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B)). Under subsection 78(4), any employee remuneration that is not paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that year, and can only be claimed as an SR&ED expenditure in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid. Under subsection 37(1.5), allowable salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada (Line 265 of Form T661) can be claimed only if: (1) the outside-Canada SR&ED work is solely in support of SR&ED carried on inside Canada by the claimant; (2) the employee is a resident of Canada; (3) the work is directly performed by the employee; and (4) the salary or wages are not subject to income or profits tax from another country. Total permissible outside-Canada salary is capped at the lesser of actual outside-Canada SR&ED salary and 10 per cent of total allowable SR&ED salaries and wages for SR&ED performed inside Canada in the taxation year, and outside-Canada salaries are excluded from the PPA salary base.
Specified Employee Restrictions and Statutory Caps

A specified employee is defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the claimant or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly, at least 10 per cent of the issued shares of any class of the claimant corporation or a related corporation. Under clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B), subsection 37(9.1), and Income Tax Regulations sections 2900(4) to 2900(10), specified employees are governed by three strict statutory caps:

items: Strict Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration: Bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to specified employees are 100 per cent excluded from allowable SR&ED salary or wages and from the PPA salary base.

Overall SR&ED Salary Cap — 5 × YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1)): The total allowable SR&ED salary or wages claimed for a specified employee (Line 305 of Form T661) cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee divided by 365. If a specified employee works for two or more associated corporations, the combined salary cap of 5 × YMPE must be allocated among the associated corporations using Form T1174.

PPA Salary Base Cap — Lesser of 75% of Salary or 2.5 × YMPE (Part 5, Section B of Form T661): When computing the salary base (Line 818) for the 55 per cent Prescribed Proxy Amount (after stripping out non-specified employee bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits on Line 812, and outside-Canada salaries), the maximum amount included for each specified employee on Line 860 is the lesser of (a) their actual SR&ED-allocated salary, capped at a maximum of 75 per cent of their total salary or wages for the year (excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits) (Line 856), and (b) the statutory formula 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365) (Line 858), where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee.

body.text: 5.3 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Transfers (Form T1146), and Third-Party Payments (Form T1263)
1. Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (80% ITC Inclusion Rule)

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), subsection 127(9) (paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure"), and the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy (updated March 30, 2022), when a claimant contracts an arm's-length party to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada (where the payer controls the work and typically retains exclusive ownership of the resulting intellectual property), 100 per cent of the eligible SR&ED contract expenditure is included in the Section 37 deductible pool (Line 340 of Form T661), while 80 per cent is included in qualified SR&ED expenditures to earn ITCs (via a 20 per cent reduction on Line 529 of Form T661). To prevent double-claiming of ITCs, the contract payment received by the arm's-length performer reduces the performer's own qualified SR&ED expenditures.

To qualify for ITCs, an arm's-length SR&ED contract must satisfy three statutory conditions: (1) the SR&ED work must be physically carried on in Canada (payments for foreign contract R&D cannot be claimed on Form T661 and earn zero ITCs); (2) the contractor must be a "taxable supplier" as defined in subsection 127(9)—meaning a person resident in Canada, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident person/partnership receiving the payment in the course of carrying on business through a permanent establishment in Canada (amounts paid to non-taxable suppliers are deducted on Line 528 of Form T661); and (3) any current contract expenditure not paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year must be excluded on Line 520 under subsection 127(26) and can only be added back (at 80 per cent on Line 500) in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid. Furthermore, under the look-through rule in subsections 37(14) and 37(15), if a performer incurs non-current expenditures under a contract when capital expenditures are ineligible, the payer's contract expenditure is reduced accordingly and the performer must notify the payer in writing within 90 days after calendar year-end.
2. Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) Contracts and Form T1146 Transfers

When a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a person or partnership with whom it does not deal at arm's length under section 251 (Line 345 of Form T661), the contract expenditure is deductible in the payer's Section 37 pool, but 0 per cent qualifies for an ITC in the hands of the payer. (Under the anti-avoidance rule in subsection 127(24), a claimant cannot circumvent this rule by interposing an arm's-length intermediary between itself and a NAL performer.) Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures and qualified expenditures, or the parties may jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsections 127(13) to 127(16) to transfer the performer's qualified expenditures to the payer (reported on Line 508 by the transferee and Line 544 by the transferor).

As detailed in Appendix A of the CRA's Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, the transferable amount on Form T1146 is strictly limited to the least of three amounts:

items: Amount 1 (Agreed Amount): The dollar amount specified by the payer and performer on Form T1146;
Amount 2 (Performer's Pool): The performer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of its taxation year (including its PPA) before deducting the transfer; and

Amount 3 (Qualifying Contract Payments Paid Within 180 Days): The total amounts that would be contract payments if the parties dealt at arm's length, provided the contract payment is paid by the payer to the performer within 180 days after the end of the performer's taxation year, and is for qualified expenditures incurred by the performer during the NAL period that are also paid by the performer within 180 days of its taxation year-end (or transferred to the performer from another NAL party). Any portion unpaid after 180 days can never be transferred in that year or any subsequent year, and partnerships cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures on Form T1146 because a partnership is not a "person" under subsection 127(13).

body.text: Additionally, when a claimant purchases goods (materials or capital property) or non-SR&ED services from a NAL supplier, subsections 127(11.5) to 127(11.8) cap the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes at the lesser of the claimant's actual outlay and the NAL supplier's adjusted selling cost or adjusted service cost (eliminating intercompany profit markups via Lines 542 and 543 of Form T661, and deeming the cost of any property originally received by the NAL supplier as a gift to be nil rather than fair market value under subsection 69(1)).
3. Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) & (ii) and Form T1263)

Under the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy (updated March 30, 2022), a payment made to an external organization for SR&ED carried on in Canada where the performer—not the payer—controls the research qualifies as a Third-Party Payment (Line 370 of Form T661, 100 per cent in the Section 37 pool and 80 per cent eligible for ITCs) if: (1) the payment is made to an Approved Entity (an approved university, college, research institute, association, or granting council), a tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada under paragraph 149(1)(j), or another Canadian-resident corporation; (2) the SR&ED relates to a business of the claimant; (3) the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED (having gained a preferential right to use the results in its business as a direct result of the payment, even though rights are non-exclusive and results are generally published); and (4) the claimant attaches a completed Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment (except for agricultural check-off dues contributed by farm producers to agricultural organizations). Unlike SR&ED contracts (which follow accrual accounting), third-party payments are claimed on a cash basis when paid, and payments in kind to universities or colleges are valued at supported fair market value.
5.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed ("Body of a Thing" Rule)

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V), Regulation 2900(2)(a), and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, materials are 100 per cent eligible for both the Section 37 deductible pool and SR&ED ITCs in the taxation year in which they are physically consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (not when purchased into inventory). Materials may be purchased from either Canadian or foreign suppliers, and their eligible cost equals the laid-down cost (invoice price plus customs and excise duties, transportation, and storage, or direct labour and production overhead for internally manufactured materials).

Because the Income Tax Act does not define "materials", the CRA strictly applies the "body of a thing" rule: "materials for SR&ED" means physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that compose the body of a tangible object ("thing") on which SR&ED is being performed or that results from the SR&ED at a given moment in the SR&ED process. Claimants must separate materials on Form T661 into two categories:

items: Materials Consumed (Line 320): Materials that are destroyed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED (such as cardboard boxes and ink destroyed in printing process tests, or seeds, agar, and chemicals rendered valueless in plant research). Materials consumed are never subject to ITC recapture.

Materials Transformed (Line 325): Physical items incorporated into another entity, prototype, custom product, or commercial asset during the SR&ED process that retain commercial value or structural identity after testing. If the transformed material or incorporating asset is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, the ITC earned on the transformed materials is subject to ITC recapture under subsection 127(27).

body.text: Crucially, laboratory supplies, glassware, and utilities that do not compose the physical body of the thing being tested—such as test tubes, pipettes, vials, beakers, flasks, petri dishes, filter papers, cleaning products, computer discs, microscopes, Bunsen burners, acids/solvents/lubricants not composing the body of the thing, and electricity or propane—do not qualify as "materials for SR&ED" (unless they are themselves the subject of the SR&ED). Under the Proxy Method, these items are covered by the 55 per cent PPA and cannot be claimed separately; under the Traditional Method, they may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead if directly related and incremental to SR&ED.
5.5 Cloud Computing, Software Licences, and Overhead Expenditures

Under the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022) and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), the eligibility of cloud computing infrastructure (such as AWS, Azure, or GCP instances), bandwidth, software licences, and indirect support costs depends on whether the claimant uses the Traditional Method or the Proxy Method:

items: Under the Traditional Method (Regulation 2900(2)(c) & Line 360): An overhead or other current expenditure qualifies on Line 360 only if it passes both the "directly related" test (requiring a direct connection, with no intervening step, to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used in SR&ED) and the "incremental" test (meaning the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred). Accordingly, cloud infrastructure spun up specifically for experimental prototypes, identifiable long-distance data/telephone charges, utilities incremental to SR&ED, Canadian testing travel and lodging, Canadian SR&ED employee training and relocation moving costs, clinical study volunteer fees, and hands-on SR&ED employee employer-paid benefits or retiring allowances can qualify on Line 360. Conversely, production cloud infrastructure, fixed monthly telephone/cellular/internet plans, headhunter and recruitment advertising fees, immigration/visa costs, fixed-cost maintenance contracts, and employer-paid benefits for clerical/administrative staff fail the directly related or incremental tests and are disallowed.

Under the Proxy Method: General overhead, SaaS subscriptions, and support utilities are covered by the 55 per cent PPA and cannot be claimed on Line 360. However, for expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, the updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy confirms that dedicated bandwidth costs (applying Data Kinetics Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 98 DTC 1877) and software licences or leased hardware dedicated to SR&ED (and not constituting General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture) may qualify as equipment lease or capital expenditures.

Prescribed Expenditures Excluded by Regulation 2902: Even if directly related and incremental to SR&ED, certain outlays are classified as prescribed expenditures under section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations and are barred from earning ITCs (reported on Lines 530 and 532 of Form T661): (1) fees paid for preparing SR&ED claims, (2) costs to attend conventions or conferences, (3) dues or fees for membership in a scientific or technical society, (4) interest and financing expenses, and (5) used capital property.

body.text: 5.6 Restored Capital Expenditures, Lease Costs, and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, capital expenditures and equipment lease costs—which had been ineligible from January 1, 2014, through December 15, 2024—were restored for depreciable property acquired (and available for use under subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024, and for lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024. The CRA issued three updated policy manuals in May and June 2026 governing these rules:
1. SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b) & Line 390 of Form T661)

Under the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), an outlay to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024, qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure under both the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III)) and the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III)) if the claimant owns (or holds a leasehold interest in) the property, the property is available for use under subsection 37(1.2), and at the time of acquisition the claimant intended either:

items: Operating Time Test: To use the property during all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada; or
Value Consumed Test: To consume all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its value in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

body.text: Capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 (and detailed in Part 6B and Line 262 of Form T661) are 100 per cent deductible in the Section 37(1)(b) pool and must not be claimed on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance). While used depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, qualifies for the Section 37(1)(b) income deduction on Line 390, used property is a prescribed expenditure under paragraph 2902(b) of the Income Tax Regulations and must be deducted on Line 532 of Form T661, earning zero ITC. Only new depreciable property earns SR&ED ITCs, and for CCPCs and ECPCs earning the 35 per cent enhanced rate, the ITC on capital expenditures is 40 per cent refundable. Land (non-depreciable), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(d).
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Subsection 127(9) & Line 504 of Form T661)

Under the SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the ≥90% ASA test because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial activities may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (claimed on Line 504 and Part 6C of Form T661) if it is actually used primarily (>50% and <90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada:

items: First-Term SUE (25% of Capital Cost): If the new equipment is actually used >50% of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period (starting when the property is available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year that occurs at least 12 months after that time), 1/4 (25 per cent) of its capital cost (excluding borrowed money costs under section 21) qualifies to earn SR&ED ITCs at the end of that taxation year.

Second-Term SUE (Additional 25% of Capital Cost): Provided the equipment qualified as First-Term SUE and is actually used >50% of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the Second Period (starting when acquired and ending at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time), an additional 1/4 (25 per cent) of its capital cost qualifies to earn SR&ED ITCs at the end of that second taxation year.

Exclusions and CCA Treatment: SUE excludes used property, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), buildings, and Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (property intended at acquisition to be used for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing facility/line and intended over its useful life to be used primarily for non-SR&ED). Unlike ≥90% ASA capital property, the capital cost of SUE is not added to the Section 37 deductible pool and is instead depreciated under regular CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8.

body.text: 3. SR&ED Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), equipment lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024, qualify as current SR&ED expenditures. Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment is used ≥90% (ASA) of its operating time in SR&ED, 100 per cent is claimed as a lease cost (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)); if used <90% of the time, the proportional SR&ED usage percentage is claimed on Line 360 as overhead if directly related and incremental (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II)). Under the Proxy Method, equipment lease costs (excluding GPOEF) are 100 per cent claimable if used ≥90% (ASA) of operating time in SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), 50 per cent claimable if used primarily (>50% to <90%) of operating time in SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), and 0 per cent claimable if used ≤50% of the time. Outlays for the use of, or right to use, a building (rent) are strictly excluded under paragraph 37(8)(d), except for prescribed special-purpose buildings approved by the Department of Finance under Regulation 2903.
6. Governing Bodies, Administrative Procedures, Prescribed Forms, and Filing Deadlines
6.1 Dual-Review Governance at the Canada Revenue Agency (RTAs and FRs)

While the Department of Finance Canada formulates tax legislation, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers all technical and financial reviews of SR&ED claims. When a claim is selected for review (which follows three phases: preparatory and planning, review, and communicating and reporting), the CRA conducts a bifurcated audit governed by two specialized procedural manuals and The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2, 2025):

items: Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs): Operating under the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors (2015-04-20), RTAs evaluate the technical eligibility of claimed projects under subsection 248(1), interviewing technical leads, reviewing contemporaneous experimental records, and verifying whether claimed support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) was commensurate with the needs of eligible R&D.

Financial Reviewers (FRs): Operating under the Financial Claim Review Manual – Review Procedures for Financial Reviewers (2018-03-15), FRs audit the financial costing on Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31, verifying payroll records, specified employee caps, 180-day payment compliance, contractor arm's-length status, government assistance reductions, and equipment usage logs.

body.text: If a claimant disagrees with a review outcome, administrative dispute resolution is governed by the CRA's Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns (2020-08-18), followed by formal Notice of Objection rights to the CRA Appeals Branch and judicial appeal to the Tax Court of Canada. Claimants also remain legally responsible for the accuracy of their claims—even if prepared by third-party consultants—and face civil penalties for overstated claims under the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025).
6.2 April 1, 2026 Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process and AI Risk Triage

Announced in Budget 2025 and officially launched by the CRA on April 1, 2026, the Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process provides businesses with optional upfront technical certainty before filing their tax return:

items: Upfront Technical Determination Within 8 Weeks: Eligible businesses can submit an application through the CRA's My Business Account portal (and request one-on-one consultations with CRA specialists) before starting work or incurring expenditures to confirm whether their planned projects qualify for SR&ED tax incentives. The CRA issues a formal technical eligibility determination within 8 weeks of receiving a complete application.

Expenditure Review Processing Cut from 180 Days to 90 Days: For claims that complete the elective pre-claim approval process and subsequently require a post-filing expenditure review, the CRA's processing time standard is cut in half from 180 days to 90 days.

AI Administration and Form T661 Consultations: Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA also expanded the use of artificial intelligence in program administration to avoid subjecting low-risk claims to unnecessary audit interventions, upgraded the SR&ED Client Portal and Self-Assessment and Learning Tool, and launched targeted consultations to modernize Form T661.

body.text: 6.4 The Strict 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline and Subsection 220(2.2)

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, as set out in the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and Guide T4088, a claimant must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information on or before 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred:

items: Corporations (18 Months After Tax Year-End): Because a corporation's income tax return filing-due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, adding the 12-month SR&ED reporting window gives a corporation exactly 18 months from the end of its taxation year to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31. If the taxation year ends on the last day of a month, the SR&ED reporting deadline is the last day of the 18th month; if the taxation year ends on a specific day within a month, the deadline falls on that exact day of the 18th month.
Individuals / Sole Proprietorships (17.5 Months After Tax Year-End): Individuals have 17.5 months from the end of the taxation year to file Form T661 and Form T2038(IND).

Partnerships: Form T661 should be filed with the partnership information return no later than 12 months after the earliest of all filing-due dates for the return of income of the members for the taxation year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends. (Where the partnership information return filing-due date applies to a mix of individual/trust and corporate partners, the partnership return itself is due on the earlier of March 31 after the calendar year in which the fiscal period ended or five months after the end of the fiscal period.)

body.text: Statutory Prohibition on Late Extensions (Subsections 37(11.1), 37(12), and 220(2.2))

If a claimant files the prescribed forms after the SR&ED reporting deadline—or fails to provide the prescribed expenditure or project information on or before that deadline—subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act removes any ministerial discretion to waive or extend the filing deadline for SR&ED prescribed forms under subsection 37(11) or paragraph 127(9)(m). Under subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12), any expenditure not reported on time on Form T661 is misclassified and deemed not to be an expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED, permanently barring the claimant from adding the outlay to the Section 37 deductible pool or earning an SR&ED ITC. The sole statutory exception is Part 9 of Form T661 (claim preparer information under paragraph 37(11)(b)): missing, incomplete, or inaccurate information in Part 9 does not disallow the SR&ED claim, but triggers a $1,000 penalty for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable.
7. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Stacking Mechanics

Every Canadian province and Yukon—except Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut, which do not offer R&D tax credits—provides a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that layers on top of the federal SR&ED program. Except for Quebec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by the Province of Alberta), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered by the CRA and require an eligible federal SR&ED claim on Form T661.
7.1 Quebec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul (Bill 6, Sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31)

In the 2025–2026 Quebec Budget (tabled March 25, 2025) and enacted into law by the Parliament of Québec in Bill 6 (An Act to give effect to fiscal measures announced in the Budget, S.Q. 2025, c. 35), Quebec consolidated its innovation tax credit system.
Abolition of Legacy Credits and Transition Date (March 25, 2025)
For taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec replaced its four legacy R&D tax credits:

items: Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (formerly section 1029.7 of the Quebec Taxation Act, Form RD-1029.7-V);
Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V);
Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V, which required a qualification certificate from the Minister of Economy, Innovation and Energy); and

Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V, subject to a grandfathering provision allowing cumulative fees or dues paid before the transition to continue generating credits for taxation years ending no later than December 31, 2029).

body.text: The New CRIC Regime (Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization)

Codified under sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31 of the Taxation Act (Quebec), the CRIC is a unified, 100 per cent refundable tax credit that can only be claimed by corporations and corporations that are members of a partnership carrying on business and maintaining an establishment in Quebec. (Sole proprietorships and individuals can no longer claim Quebec R&D tax credits for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025.)
The statutory design of the Quebec CRIC comprises five core elements:

items: Two-Tier Refundable Rates (30% and 20%) with No Asset Cap: The CRIC provides an enhanced 30 per cent refundable rate on up to $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures exceeding the annual exclusion threshold, and a 20 per cent base refundable rate on eligible expenditures above that $1,000,000 limit. No asset-based eligibility test is required to access the 30 per cent enhanced rate. The $1,000,000 enhanced limit must be shared among associated corporations using Form RD-1029.8.EN, is prorated for short taxation years based on the number of days in the year, and does not apply where a corporation claims its share of expenditures as a member of a partnership (which earns the 20 per cent base rate).

Annual Exclusion Threshold ($50,000 Minimum Floor): Eligible expenditures must exceed an exclusion threshold defined as the greater of (a) $50,000 adjusted for the number of days in the taxation year, or (b) an employee-based threshold calculated using the basic personal amount applicable to the employees devoted to the eligible activities.

Expanded Eligible Activities — R&D Plus Pre-Commercialization: In addition to pure research, applied research, and experimental development, the CRIC covers eligible pre-commercialization activities performed in Quebec as a continuation of R&D—specifically including testing, prototyping, technological validation, studies required for initial regulatory approval or certification, and product design (shape, aesthetics, functional features, and material selection).

Eligible Expenditure Categories: Eligible costs under the CRIC include: (a) 100 per cent of salaries and wages of employees engaged in R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Quebec (including direct support roles); (b) 50 per cent of amounts paid to arm's-length subcontractors reasonably attributable to work performed in Quebec; (c) 50 per cent of payments made to an eligible public research centre, research consortium, or university entity in Quebec; and (d) capital expenditures for brand-new depreciable equipment (excluding land, buildings, and rights in a building) available for use in Quebec almost exclusively in eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities.

Revenu Québec Forms and CO-17 Reporting Codes: Claimants file Form RD-1029.8.CR (CRIC claim) and Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures) with their CO-17 corporate return (or within 12 months after the CO-17 filing deadline, i.e., 18 months after tax year-end), reporting the credit under Code 112 (R&D portion) and Code 113 (Pre-commercialization portion).

body.text: 7.2 Ontario: Three-Tier R&D Tax Credit System (Taxation Act, 2007)

Corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment (defined via Regulation 400) performing SR&ED in Ontario can claim three separate provincial tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario, S.O. 2007, c. 11), all administered by the CRA:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Taxation Act, 2007): An 8 per cent refundable tax credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (100% of current expenditures, 80% of arm's-length contracts/third-party payments, 55% PPA, and—for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024—restored capital expenditures) up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 shared among associated corporations (maximum annual cash refund of $240,000). (Ontario left its OITC limit at $3,000,000 when the federal limit rose to $6,000,000.) The $3,000,000 limit is reduced by two phase-out grinds: (a) when prior-year federal taxable income of the associated group is between $500,000 and $800,000, and (b) when prior-year specified capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Claimed on Schedule 566 (T2SCH566) (Line 468 of Schedule 5) and may be waived in whole or in part under subsection 96(14).

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38 to 45, Taxation Act, 2007): A 3.5 per cent non-refundable tax credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (including restored capital property acquired on or after December 16, 2024) with no expenditure cap, available to offset Ontario corporate income tax otherwise payable and carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years. Under Section 41, the OITC is government assistance that reduces the expenditure base on which the 3.5 per cent ORDTC is calculated. Claimed on Schedule 508 (T2SCH508) (Line 416 of Schedule 5) and may be waived under Section 43.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Taxation Act, 2007): A 20 per cent refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under an eligible contract with an Ontario Eligible Research Institute (ERI)—including Ontario universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, Ontario Centres of Excellence, and Networks of Centres of Excellence—up to an annual qualified expenditure cap of $20,000,000 (maximum annual cash credit of $4,000,000). Claimed on Schedule 568 (T2SCH568), accompanied by a separate Schedule 569 (T2SCH569) for each eligible contract, and entered on Line 470 of Schedule 5.
